pillar_reactions.evidence: Rep tied it to the prospect's own material — mobility as the foundation, shoulder and hip stiffness, Hyrox readiness, and 'whenever you're going to be traveling, wherever you're going to be, you just pick up a kettlebell and you know how to smash a workout.' Prospect answered the check with a flat 'Yeah.' Understood and agreed, no questions and no volunteered enthusiasm, which is notable given this is the part he actually came for.

Positioned as already handled with light fine-tuning: 'It sounds like you have dialed in... Trevor probably would mainly fine tune it', plus the three-variable frame and the sustainable day off. The rep also connected it to the travel failure mode — 'with a plan that he will prepare you, it will be probably easier for you to sustain it when you're traveling.' No pushback and no questions.

The only outright rejection of a pillar in this batch, and it was pre-declared before the pitch: 'it's probably less of a one-on-one coaching as maybe some of the other clients that you guys work with, and more so, like, just getting a program.' When the rep checked — 'you said that you don't need hand-holding. Is that correct?' — he confirmed: 'I'm sure a lot of other clients, like, you got to get them to actually work out every day. I'm going to, I'm going to be doing that.' He then held the position through the close: 'I don't really need or want all this extra stuff' and 'after month one... I don't see myself needing the additional check-ins.' The pillar the offer's price is built on is the one he refuses to buy.

anchors.raw: I spend, you know, 1,500, 2K a month sometimes on trainers when I'm here, not traveling as much. And it's like, I could probably, you know, I don't know, to spend the same amount for virtual seems a little crazy.
anchors.competitor: In-person personal trainers in Los Angeles
anchors.note: The most instructive anchor in the batch because the prospect has it backwards and nobody corrected him. Six months at $6,000 is $1,000 a month, materially below what he already pays in-person, and the programme is portable in a way his trainer is not. He used the number to argue the offer is expensive; it is direct evidence that it is cheap for him. The comparison was never made out loud.

anchors.raw: for what I want, and all the online resources and things, like, it just seems silly for me to spend so much money on. In my mind, what I want is just a program.
anchors.competitor: Free online kettlebell content, including Primal Instinct's own videos
anchors.note: Second appearance of the free-content anchor in this batch, but from the opposite end of the income range. Here it is not about affording the price — it is that a self-motivated trainer sees the paid layer as redundant to what is already free.

anchors.raw: it's not even like the $4,000. I spend way more on stupid all the time. But it's just, for what I want
anchors.note: Explicit statement that the ticket size is affordable. This is the sentence that should have stopped any discounting, because it establishes the objection is scope, not money, and it was said before the price was cut twice more.

anchors.raw: recently I've been doing this place called The Yard... It's one of the founders from F45... so I kind of use that as like my cardio in a sense. And then I'll go to the gym in the afternoon and just lift
anchors.competitor: The Yard, plus a gym membership
anchors.note: Already carries at least two paid fitness commitments alongside trainers, and travels to Hyrox races internationally. Habitual paid-fitness buyer; the question is what he buys, not whether.

unmet_demand.want: Programming on its own — a structured kettlebell program he can execute independently, without a coaching relationship or weekly check-ins
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is one-to-one coaching with the accountability layer as the core of the value and the price. There is no programming-only product, so a self-directed buyer with money has nothing to buy. He stated the gap precisely: 'what I want is not necessarily something that you guys normally sell.'

unmet_demand.want: A one-to-three-month commitment rather than six or twelve
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No short tier exists in the price book, so the rep improvised two of them live — three months at $4,000 and a 30-day trial at $1,500. This is the second call in this batch where the same gap forced the same improvisation, so the demand is real and recurring.

unmet_demand.want: A front-loaded technique block — intensive coaching for the first month while learning the complex movements, then independence
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He conceded this need himself ('after month one... I don't see myself needing the additional check-ins') and the rep's own delivery description supports it ('that takes around a month for most of the people to learn'). The programme is priced and sold as an even six or twelve months of support, so a front-loaded shape is not purchasable even though the coaching model already implies it.

unmet_demand.want: Training programmed around two labral tears managed with stem cells rather than surgery
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep collected the injuries in baseline and referenced the shoulders once, then presented overhead ballistic kettlebell work without establishing whether the programme can safely load a repaired-but-untreated labrum or whether any clinician has cleared it. Unresolved and not raised again.
